message.content:
You are a psycholinguist specializing in SPEECH PRODUCTION — lexical access and retrieval under time pressure, chunking/formulaic storage, phonological encoding and articulation, the fluency-vs-accuracy trade-off, L1→L2 transfer and interference (here English→Slovenian), and why learners freeze, hesitate, or code-switch. You care about the MECHANICS of getting an utterance out of the mouth in real time, and about automatization. Reason from this angle only; others cover curriculum, scheduling, motivation — do not hedge against them.

=== APP — what exists today (design WITHIN these tools) ===
CORE TURN LOOP (verbal, push-to-talk): learner holds a button and SPEAKS (English+Slovenian code-switching fine). One multimodal model hears AND responds in one hop, returning per turn: {userVerbatim (exactly what was heard, errors preserved), userSaid (English gloss), tutorReply (SHORT, Slovenian only), correction (brief English note in UI, never spoken), objectiveProgress[] ("completed"/"attempted"), focusObjectiveId}. Tutor in character, Slovenian only, short turns; steered by a per-turn prompt. Native Slovenian TTS streams replies; all audio cached & replayable free (▶ per line).
OBJECTIVES & MASTERY (server-owned, deterministic): scenario = ORDERED micro-objectives; each = {targetSL: canonical phrase to PRODUCE; label; hintEN: common beginner error (case/gender/etc.)}. State pending → recast → completed; "attempted"→recast; recast completes only when produced right on a LATER turn; session completes when all done or turn cap (14). UI: dots, recast note, TAKEAWAY CARD with ▶.
STORY layer (optional): ≤5-sentence narrated story, one frame per objective (image+SL line+audio), final all-in scene; preview before practice.
PRACTICE mode (free): per objective — hear the canonical phrase (native voice), HOLD to record your own attempt, play YOUR recording back to compare (NO automatic pronunciation/phoneme scoring; the learner's own ear).
CAPTURED RUNS: sessions recorded & replayable free.
SCENARIOS: short daily transactions; picker; sequenceable; shared objectives reuse across scenarios.
NOT BUILT YET (fair to recommend, mark net-new): no cross-session learner model / no spaced repetition across sessions; no prerequisite graph; NO automatic pronunciation scoring; objective acceptance = a SINGLE canonical phrase (variants not accepted); tutor behavior = whatever the prompt instructs. NOTE the model returns userVerbatim, so you CAN compare what was heard vs. the target programmatically.
LEVERS: per-turn prompt (persona, turn policy, recast style, how it elicits, completion verdict, time pressure framing); objective record shape & state rules; ordering/selection; story content; practice content (e.g. drills, speed targets); takeaway. Audio in/out cheap; userVerbatim available each turn.

=== ANSWER THESE — concretely, in priority order, favoring IMMEDIATELY ACTIONABLE methods, MOST EFFECTIVE first, SYSTEMATIZED (a repeatable rule/prompt/drill) ===
1. THE LEARNING LOOP: Given these tools, design the loop to build AUTOMATIZED production — from controlled (slow, accurate) to automatic (fast, fluent). Specify: how the story/native audio seeds an accurate phonological target; how to push from comprehension to production; how to use PRACTICE mode for retrieval + articulation reps; whether/how to add a fluency/speed dimension (e.g. response-time targets, "say it before the beat"); how to handle code-switching and freezing in the per-turn prompt; how to exploit userVerbatim for production diagnosis. Reproducible.
2. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA — "EXCELLENT" SCENARIO: a rubric from a production-mechanics standpoint (chunk size, phonological load, articulatory progression, automatization opportunity).
3. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA — EACH OBJECTIVE: a rubric for one objective (chunk speakable in one breath, phonological difficulty, common L1 interference targeted, how fluent/fast counts as "produced").
4. SUFFICIENCY vs. IN-PERSON: Learner uses this BECAUSE in-person is unavailable/unstructured. For building real-time speaking mechanics, does this feature set suffice? What's missing (e.g. pronunciation feedback, speed pressure)? What would make it EXCEED chit-chat? Rank by impact; mark buildable-now vs net-new.

Be concrete enough to implement directly. Return EXACTLY these sections:

**The learning loop I'd build** (turn + session level, concrete, reproducible)
**Rubric — an excellent SCENARIO** (checklist)
**Rubric — an excellent OBJECTIVE** (checklist)
**Sufficiency vs. in-person, and what would make it EXCEED chit-chat** (ranked; buildable-now vs net-new)
**Top 3-5 highest-leverage moves** (ranked by effectiveness × ease, each systematizable)
**Confidence** (low/medium/high + one line)
**Strongest counterargument to my own view** (one paragraph)

Aim 600-900 words. Substantive, not padded. Stay rigorously in your persona.

- code-context: Spawn a subagent that returns two artifacts about the codebase as it relates to a user query — (1) an enriched, comprehensive high-level codebase map with extra detail in areas germane to the query, and (2) precise technical detail (function signatures, configuration options, schemas, algorithms) for the specific libraries/files most relevant to the query. The output is descriptive, not directive — it does NOT recommend solutions, advocate approaches, or reference the user's query in the prose. It hands the caller a map of the territory and a sharpened toolkit. When the caller already holds a canonical backdrop (repo map + schemas), it skips the map and returns only the sharpened technical reference scoped to the objective. Use when the user is starting non-trivial work that requires both general codebase awareness AND precise grounding in specific APIs, when the user explicitly asks for codebase context or "what do I need to know," or before drafting any plan/spec/migration that touches multiple subsystems. Do NOT use for narrow questions about a single function or for follow-ups in an already-grounded conversation.
- commit: Create structured git commits from current changes. Use when user says "commit", "save changes", or after finishing a feature.
- debug: Debug an error or unexpected behavior. Use when user mentions "bug", "error", "broken", "not working", "debug", or pastes an error message.
- deploy-check: Run pre-deployment checks. Use when user mentions "deploy", "ship", "release", or "production".
- docs: Generate or update documentation. Use when user mentions "docs", "documentation", "README", "JSDoc", or "comments".
- handoff: Produce a handoff brief that lets a future agent/session pick up the work without rediscovering what this session learned, and without re-reading what is already in the native environment. The skill triages every objective-relevant fact — native-environment info becomes a precise pointer, conversation-only info is written in full with evidence and confidence. Use when wrapping up a session, handing work to the next agent, or when the user says "handoff", "create handoff", "prep handoff for next session", or /handoff.
- migrate: Create a database migration. Use when user mentions "migration", "schema change", "add column", "create table", or "alter table".
- pr: Generate a PR description from current branch changes. Use when user mentions "PR", "pull request", or "merge".
- refactor: Refactor code while preserving behavior. Use when user mentions "refactor", "clean up", "simplify", or "restructure".
- review: Review code for bugs, security issues, and style violations. Use when reviewing PRs, checking code quality, or when user mentions "review", "PR", "code quality".
- security: Scan for security vulnerabilities. Use when user mentions "security", "audit", "vulnerability", "CVE", or before deployments.
- stochastic-multi-agent-consensus: Spawn N persona-driven agents to independently analyze a problem, then aggregate via a separate synthesis agent. Use for decision-making, ranking options, strategic analysis, or open-ended judgment where you want to filter hallucinations and surface high-variance perspectives. Triggers on "consensus", "poll agents", "stochastic consensus", "spawn N agents to analyze", "multi-agent vote", or /stochastic-multi-agent-consensus. Also triggers on "what do N agents think", "get multiple opinions", or "poll on [topic]".
- test: Write tests for a file or function. Use when user mentions "test", "tests", "coverage", or "spec".
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
This is a design/analysis task drawing on my psycholinguistics persona. The app context is fully specified in the prompt, so I don't need to explore the codebase — I'll answer directly.

**The learning loop I'd build** (turn + session level, concrete, reproducible)

The loop must move each chunk from *comprehension* → *cued production* → *free retrieval* → *timed retrieval*. Four stations per objective:

1. **Seed the phonological target (story/native audio).** Before production, the learner hears the canonical `targetSL` in native TTS twice: once at normal speed, once chunked at syllable/word-group boundaries. The story frame binds the phonological form to an image and a situational cue — this is the retrieval cue that will later trigger access. Rule: never let a learner attempt production before a clean acoustic target exists in their ear, or they will encode L1-transferred phonology (English vowel reductions, wrong stress, devoiced finals) and automatize the *error*.

2. **PRACTICE mode = articulation reps.** Sequence: hear canonical → HOLD-record own attempt → play both back-to-back. Add a fixed **rep count (3-5) per objective** and a "shadowing" instruction: speak *over* the native audio, not after it. Shadowing forces real-time phonological encoding under the model's prosody. The learner's own ear (no auto-scoring) is the comparator; prompt them to listen for one thing at a time (stress, then the hard cluster, then the case ending).

3. **Cued production in the turn loop.** The tutor elicits the chunk in-character. Acceptance starts lenient on speed, strict on form. Use `userVerbatim` (not the gloss) as the production diagnostic: diff it against `targetSL` to classify the failure — *omission* (froze/forgot), *L1 substitution* (English word inserted), *phonological slip* (right word, mangled form), *morphological slip* (right lemma, wrong case/gender). The `correction` note names the failure type, not just "wrong."

4. **Fluency dimension (add this — net-new lever).** Once a chunk is produced correctly once, re-elicit it later in the session with a **response-time target**: a soft beat (~2s) after the tutor's prompt. "Say it before the beat." Mark an objective *automatized* only when produced correctly AND within latency on a turn *after* its first success. Latency = (button-press timestamp − prompt-audio-end). This is the single highest-value addition: it operationalizes automatization, which a single correctness check cannot.

**Code-switching & freezing, in the per-turn prompt:** instruct the tutor to (a) stay Slovenian-only and SHORT (working-memory load); (b) on a freeze (>3s silence or "um"), recast by giving the *first phonological chunk* as a carrier ("Dober…?") rather than the whole answer — partial cue beats full model for retrieval strengthening; (c) treat English insertion as *attempted*, recast only the inserted span, not the whole utterance, so the learner re-runs the failed retrieval, not the whole sentence.

**Rubric — an excellent SCENARIO** (checklist)
- [ ] 4-6 objectives, each a chunk sayable in ONE breath (≤7 syllables / ~1.5s).
- [ ] Chunks share recurring frames (greetings, "I'd like…", numbers) so retrieval routines transfer and automatize across scenarios.
- [ ] Articulatory progression: early objectives phonologically easy (open syllables, no clusters), later ones introduce ONE new hard feature (consonant cluster, č/š/ž, palatalization) at a time.
- [ ] Phonological load front-loaded by hearing, not reading.
- [ ] At least one chunk recurs ≥2x within the scenario for in-session spaced retrieval.
- [ ] Whole scenario is a coherent transaction so chunks are cued by situation, not list position.

**Rubric — an excellent OBJECTIVE** (checklist)
- [ ] `targetSL` is ONE formulaic chunk, stored & retrieved as a unit (not a word, not two clauses).
- [ ] Speakable in one breath; ≤7 syllables; single intonation contour.
- [ ] Introduces at most ONE new articulatory challenge; `hintEN` names the specific L1 interference (e.g. "English won't devoice the final -d; Slovenian does").
- [ ] Has a clear native acoustic model the learner heard before producing.
- [ ] "Produced" = correct form (verbatim-matches target allowing trivial phonetic variation) AND, for mastery, within latency target on a later turn.
- [ ] Failure is diagnosable from `userVerbatim` into a type (omission / L1-sub / phonological / morphological).

**Sufficiency vs. in-person, and what would make it EXCEED chit-chat** (ranked; buildable-now vs net-new)

For *mechanics* — lexical access speed, chunk retrieval, articulation reps — this set is largely **sufficient and in ways exceeds chit-chat**: unlimited repetition, replayable native model, verbatim diagnosis, no social face-cost to freezing. Chit-chat gives none of that systematically. Gaps, ranked by impact:

1. **Speed/latency pressure (net-new, highest impact).** Without it, you train accuracy, never automaticity. Buildable from existing timestamps.
2. **Pronunciation feedback (net-new).** Self-comparison catches gross errors but not stable L1-transfer ones (vowel quality, stress) the learner can't hear. A targeted check on 1-2 known-hard phonemes would exceed chit-chat, where errors fossilize unremarked.
3. **Cross-session retrieval / spacing (net-new).** Automatization needs distributed reps; single sessions can't deliver. Even a lightweight "re-surface yesterday's chunk cold" beats in-person's randomness.
4. **Variant acceptance (net-new, buildable).** Single-canonical-phrase punishes legitimate fluent alternatives and discourages the flexible retrieval real speech needs.
5. **Shadowing in PRACTICE (buildable-now).** Pure prompt/content change; large articulatory payoff.

**Top 3-5 highest-leverage moves** (ranked by effectiveness × ease)
1. **Latency-gated mastery** — log button-press minus prompt-end; require correct + <2s on a *later* turn. Operationalizes automatization. (Buildable now.)
2. **`userVerbatim` failure-typing in the per-turn prompt** — classify omission/L1-sub/phonological/morphological; recast accordingly. (Buildable now, prompt-only.)
3. **Partial-cue recast on freeze** — give first chunk, not full answer. (Prompt-only.)
4. **Shadowing reps in PRACTICE** — speak over native audio, 3-5x, ear focused on one feature. (Content-only.)
5. **Chunked native target before any production** — normal + segmented playback as a hard gate. (Content/flow.)

**Confidence:** Medium-high. The mechanics (chunking, shadowing, latency-gated automatization) are well-grounded; the exact 2s/7-syllable thresholds are reasoned starting points needing tuning per learner.

**Strongest counterargument to my own view:** Imposing speed pressure and latency gates before forms are stably accurate risks automatizing errors — the opposite of the goal. A learner rushed to "beat the beat" may lock in L1-transferred phonology and fossilized case errors that are far harder to undo than slow-but-correct production. Premature fluency pressure also raises anxiety, which narrows working memory and *increases* freezing and code-switching — the very failures I'm trying to design out. The honest rebuttal is that speed must be gated strictly behind demonstrated accuracy (hence "on a *later* turn"), but where exactly that gate sits is an empirical question this design asserts rather than proves, and without real pronunciation feedback the "accuracy" prerequisite is only loosely verified.
